titulo.texto: Mural “The Magical World of the Maya,” by Leonora Carrington

frase_gancho.texto: A Surrealist painter traveled to Chiapas to paint the Maya world.

puente_narrativo.texto: From the cold mountain we have come down to the hot jungle. Look for a clay vessel with the face of a god modeled on the front, made for burning copal.

guion_corto.texto: This mural, small for such a monumental museum, was painted by the British artist Leonora Carrington, one of the great figures of Surrealism, who lived most of her life in Mexico. In 1963, Ignacio Bernal, the museum’s first director, commissioned her to create a work for the hall dedicated to Chiapas. She traveled to the region, drew the people and animals she saw, and read the Popol Vuh, the sacred book of the K’iche’ Maya. She stayed in San Cristóbal de las Casas with the Swiss anthropologist Gertrude Blom, who introduced her to two healers from Zinacantán who allowed her to attend their ceremonies. The result is a personal vision in which the everyday and the magical blend together.

guion_largo.texto:
It is easy to walk right past this mural, and that would be a shame. It is small for a museum of enormous buildings and monuments, but it has a big story: that of a European artist who let the mountains of Chiapas carry her away and tried to paint what she saw, and what she dreamed, of the Maya world.

Leonora Carrington was born in England in 1917, arrived in Mexico in the 1940s, and stayed until her death in 2011. She was one of the great figures of Surrealism, the movement that mixes reality with dreams. Her paintings are full of animals, fantastic creatures, and scenes where nothing is quite what it seems. In Mexico City she was a close friend of another Surrealist painter, Remedios Varo.

In 1963, when the museum was getting ready to open, its first director, Ignacio Bernal, commissioned her to paint a mural for the hall dedicated to Chiapas. It was no ordinary commission: the museum brought together many artists from across the country so that, alongside the archaeological and ethnographic pieces, there would be works from its own time. Carrington was given the task of painting the Maya world.

Before picking up the brush, she went to Chiapas. She stayed in San Cristóbal de las Casas, at the home of the Swiss anthropologist Gertrude Blom, who knew the region very well. Blom introduced her to two healers from Zinacantán, a Tzotzil town in the Highlands, who allowed her to attend some of their ceremonies. Carrington made drawings of the people and animals of the place.

She also read the Popol Vuh, the sacred book of the K’iche’ Maya, to understand the beliefs from before the conquest. There it is told, among many other things, that the gods tried to create humans from mud and from wood, until they succeeded with maize. It is the same book of the twins who play ball against the lords of death, whom you have already met in the Gulf Hall and in the Maya Hall.

Her mural is not a copy of anything. Surrealism seeks precisely to erase the border between the real and the dreamed, and in the Highlands of Chiapas she found a world where ceremonies, animals, and sacred mountains are part of the same life. It is a personal vision, that of someone who looked from the outside, and for that very reason it reminds us that there are many ways of seeing.

Think of the wool tunic you just saw. Chamula and Zinacantán, the two Tzotzil towns of the Highlands, are neighbors. A garment and a mural are two different ways of telling the story of the same place.

Before moving on, give it a minute. Count the animals you find, look at what the people are doing, and ask yourself what seems real and what seems like a dream. In that doubt, in the border between what is seen and what is believed, lies the very magic that Carrington wanted to paint. It is one of those works the museum keeps quietly, and it changes how you look at the rest of the hall.

texto: Count the animals you find in the painting
Look at the people: what are they doing or wearing?
Notice the colors and shapes: what seems real and what seems like a dream?

texto.Author: Leonora Carrington (1917-2011)
texto.Commission: Ignacio Bernal, first director of the museum

texto.pregunta: Myth: The museum’s murals were painted only by Indigenous artists or artists from ancient times.
texto.respuesta: Reality: There are works by twentieth-century artists, such as the British Surrealist Leonora Carrington, who traveled to Chiapas to paint this mural.
